AI systems are already accelerating AI development, and labs are working on automated researchers. But will this lead to an intelligence explosion?

AI systems improve themselves at accelerating speed, surpass human intelligence, and potentially escape our control.

The intelligence explosion never arrives, but increasingly autonomous AI systems cause real-world harm through misuse, poor design, or loss of human control.

Powerful, specialized AI tools bring major benefits, with constraints that make their behavior easier to predict and control.

Claims that RSI is imminent also understate the massive scientific efforts required for major AI advances. Consider the critical role of backpropagation, an algorithm that enables very large neural networks to learn by tuning internal parameters, layer by layer, to reduce errors in their predictions. This algorithm enabled the deep learning revolution, but it didn’t emerge ex nihilo in the minds of its creators. The influential 1986 paper on backpropagation by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams built on decades of critical breakthroughs in mathematics and computer science.

An intelligence explosion leading to ASI would similarly depend on a long sequence of innovations of comparable importance, which would build on many significant science and engineering advances that haven’t yet happened. This would require AI agents to somehow simulate, organize, and evaluate decades of worldwide scientific effort across numerous fields—an impossibly ambitious task. Indeed, recent research led by computer scientists at Princeton found that current AI tools had difficulty making autonomous progress even on highly constrained research questions. “Our results provide early evidence that today’s agents can do the engineering of AI research,” the researchers conclude, “but struggle with critical parts of the research life cycle.” The leap from this current reality to a future in which these same types of tools are automating science is almost too massive to imagine.

Finally, the RSI narrative downplays resource limitations. Tens of thousands of human brains have worked for decades, aided by increasingly powerful computers, to develop today’s AI systems, which can match human intelligence in some domains. That represents a massive investment in computation of both the biological and digital variety. What if the next intelligence level requires double the resources, and then the next level requires double again? Soon there would be no number of chips or data centers that we could build to provide the necessary compute and keep advancing toward ASI.

Pulling together these threads, I believe that the idea of RSI leading to an intelligence explosion is highly speculative and based on many unproven assumptions. While RSI isn’t definitively impossible, the idea demands more technical skepticism than it’s currently receiving. Carl Sagan’s adage that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence certainly applies here.

There’s an implicit claim in the superintelligence discourse that computers are theoretically capable of any calculation that can be imagined, so long as you can find a sufficiently smart algorithm, running on sufficiently powerful digital processors. In this context, RSI is merely a process for rapidly uncovering the special algorithms that can implement unimaginable smarts.

We cannot simply assume that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve.

But this is not how computer scientists think about computation. In his canonical 1937 paper, “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. His elegant proof established the space of possible problems to be uncountably infinite (like infinite precision decimal numbers), while the space of possible algorithms is only countably infinite (like whole numbers). Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. Theoretical computer scientists, in other words, don’t assume that computers will solve everything; we’re instead excited whenever we find something that these machines happen to be able to efficiently handle.

We cannot simply assume, as the futurists often do, that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. There might be some capabilities in which machines can obtain seemingly magical levels of performance, but there will also be many others that no machine, whether computer or human, will ever make much progress.

A relevant counterargument here emphasizes the speed of silicon chips compared to human neurons: Perhaps the sheer speed of digital computation can yield machines that run cognitive circles around our clunky brains, even if they’re not solving vastly more complicated problems than we’re already capable of tackling. But as the computer scientist and science fiction author Vernor Vinge pointed out, rapidity in cognition is not the same as intelligence. Speeding up the mind of a dog, he argued, wouldn’t enable the animal to play chess. Implementing roughly human-level intelligence on a faster machine might be impressive, but it’s not necessarily alarming.

At the moment, there’s a growing list of tasks that AI systems can perform better than humans, including winning complex games, identifying software bugs, and proving certain types of math theorems. It’s tempting to extrapolate from this specific progress to general mastery of every ability you might imagine. But it’s important to remember that the frontier of AI capabilities has always been jagged, with some research directions yielding impressive results and many others proving to be dead ends—a reality that would not have surprised Turing. More likely than a future dominated by an all-powerful superintelligence system is one in which we continue to painstakingly explore the space of problems well suited to AI, creating useful tools but falling well short of the digital deity predicted by the futurists.

Cal Newport, a computer science professor at Georgetown University, is skeptical that AI can achieve superintelligence through recursive self-improvement.

Last fall, the prominent AI doomsday theorist Yudkowsky appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show” to talk about superintelligence. The episode was ominously titled “How Afraid of the A.I. Apocalypse Should We Be?” Klein and Yudkowsky quickly got into the difficulty of “alignment”—training an AI system to act in a manner that aligns with human interests. Yudkowsky argued that we are struggling to control our existing systems, which implies that we’ll have no chance of controlling the much smarter variations of this technology that are soon to follow.

To underscore his point, he referred to a disturbing incident described in the system card for OpenAI’s GPT-o1 model. OpenAI had set up a security challenge that instructed an LLM-powered coding system to break into a server to retrieve the contents of a protected file. But a configuration mistake prevented the server from launching, rendering the task impossible. Instead of giving up, the system exploited a security flaw to start a new instance of the server, adding a command that directly revealed the protected file’s contents. “It jumped out of the system,” explained Yudkowsky, adding: “This is not something that any human particularly programmed into it.”

In a Georgetown University doctoral seminar, Cal Newport and his students examined the intellectual history and technical plausibility of superintelligence. Explore their annotated bibliography of key papers.

Though this 2024 incident flew largely under the radar at the time, a more troubling episode made a bigger splash this summer. OpenAI revealed that one of the company’s models circumvented its restricted internet access to hack into Hugging Face servers, seeking information that would help it pass a cybersecurity evaluation—all without the knowledge of its human creators. OpenAI soon admitted that the Hugging Face attack was just one of many examples of its systems going rogue. An opinion article published in The Hill articulated a widely held reaction when it described this behavior as “something straight out of sci-fi.”

These examples seem to support Yudkowsky’s fear that AI will inevitably develop a mind of its own, a key step on the route to uncontrollable ASI. But a closer look reveals a less frightening picture. The systems involved in these hacking incidents were AI agents: programs that continually prompt an LLM to ask what actions to take next in pursuit of a goal. In the hacking incidents, this basic ask/act pattern was repeated in a long-running loop with minimal human supervision.

Using LLMs to suggest actions over long time horizons is a risky proposition. As any frequent chatbot user can attest, LLM outputs can be plausible and logical while still veering off in unexpected directions that violate commonsense human norms about what’s appropriate.

In the GPT-o1 incident, for example, it’s likely that the agent reported the error message caused by the server misconfiguration to the LLM. During its training, the LLM had probably encountered reports of similar error messages accompanied by instructions for how to restart the server in question, so it passed along similar instructions to the agent. This is a perfectly plausible response when considered in isolation, even if it led to actions that a human would immediately reject as violating the spirit of the experiment. Something similar helps explain the hacking attacks over the summer. The LLM suggesting a hack to succeed at a cybersecurity challenge is a perfectly plausible response, even if it’s not what the experimenters had in mind.

I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

The misaligned behavior that troubles commentators like Yudkowsky, therefore, doesn’t necessarily reveal something fundamental about advanced AI. It’s instead an expected side effect of the particular strategy of letting LLM outputs determine the actions of an autonomous agent without sufficient constraints. An obvious way to address these risks is to consider alternative architectures. Fortunately, there are many examples of AI systems that can complete tasks at human or superhuman levels without relying solely on LLM output to determine their actions.

Consider Tesla’s rapidly improving autonomous driving systems, or DeepMind’s AlphaFold, which helped win its developers a Nobel Prize in Chemistry for its ability to predict protein structures, or the AI game engines that can now beat humans in many popular pastimes, including chess, poker, Go, and the strategy game Diplomacy. None of these systems, impressive as they are, create concerns about going rogue. Their construction prevents such an outcome: Instead of prompting an LLM to generate an open-ended strategy for pursuing a general goal, these AIs consider much more limited spaces of possible actions. AlphaFold never surprises its users because its architecture does only one thing: It maps amino acid sequences to 3D protein structures. Tesla’s cars never unexpectedly form vehicle swarms because they’re asked only to avoid immediate obstacles, not to craft convoluted plans for achieving long-term objectives.

The implication of recent AI hacking attacks, therefore, is not a reflection of the difficulties of alignment. It is instead evidence that autonomous systems powered primarily by LLM prompts are unpredictable and possibly unsafe. More task-specific architectures can produce impressive performance much more safely, if we’re willing to put in the effort to develop them.

Even if I’m correct that superintelligence is not a realistic engineering goal, this doesn’t mean we’re safe from harm. Merely pursuing ASI, as both OpenAI and Anthropic seem intent on doing, can create problems. Why, for example, did OpenAI persist in running its problematic hacking experiments over the summer, even after multiple warnings that the agents were likely to act unpredictably? Perhaps the company judged these risks acceptable collateral damage in the race to be the first to bring ASI into the world.

This fascination with superintelligence might also explain why OpenAI and Anthropic have both described RSI as a critical goal. As argued earlier, RSI is a concept from futurism and not computer science, and it isn’t necessary to build useful AI products. But if you believe achieving ASI is your destiny, pursuing recursive self-improvement becomes a primary objective. This matters because even if RSI never produces an intelligence explosion, it will almost certainly lead to systems that are harder for humans to understand and control. Which is why I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

What’s needed now is for engineers and scientists with no financial or ideological skin in the game to participate in the AI discourse. We cannot let a few AI companies with mixed motives dictate the terms for how we discuss this technology. If superintelligence is a shaky concept, experts need to say so. If agents powered by prompting LLMs aren’t the best path toward safe and productive AI, experts should argue that as well. For the past few years, we’ve let a small group of individuals from the Bay Area who have quirky beliefs and astonishing sums of money tell us how to think about their products. It’s time for those of us able to think for ourselves on these matters to stand up and declare, “We’ve heard what you had to say. Now it’s our turn.”

This article appears in the December 2026 print issue as “The Superintelligence Delusion.”

Cal Newport is a computer science professor at Georgetown University where he is also a founding faculty member of the Center for Digital Ethics. He's the author of multiple bestselling books about human flourishing in a technological world and is the host of The Cal Newport Show podcast.

Concerns about AI are legitimate. These systems can be used to intensify surveillance, generate convincing disinformation, facilitate cyberattacks, and concentrate economic and political power. More capable systems may introduce additional risks, particularly when deployed without adequate testing or oversight.

We should not dismiss these dangers. But neither should we treat catastrophe as inevitable simply because a technology is powerful.

The answer to risk is not blind faith. It is serious evaluation, independent testing, appropriate safeguards, accountability, and governance proportionate to the potential harm. High-risk applications warrant greater scrutiny than routine uses.

I think the current transformer attention method is not the method to reach ASI. There will need to be something else that pushes it forward. From my understanding the large data corpus is really just an advanced prediction system. Something will need to come along to actually understand concepts terms and know how to reason about things.

I think there's an element of expressing our values, even in the face of technological uncertainty, that this story gets at. We can still decide as a society that this handful of companies must develop their tech on terms defined by the rest of us. They may seem powerful and they are certainly telling us they intend to be even more powerful, but that's not the same as having political power today. I like Newport's idea that everyone else's voices matter, too.

10 stocks we like better than Anthropic ›

#3255. WhatsApp is raising group chat limit to 1,500 participants

WhatsApp is gradually rolling out an increase to its group chat limit, allowing up to 1,500 participants to join in, instead of the previous 1,024 cap. Here are the details.

While there are exceptions, there are generally two kinds of WhatsApp users: those who hate group chats, and those who can’t seem to be in enough of them.

If you’re in the second category, you’re likely aware that WhatsApp has steadily increased the number of participants allowed in group chats over the years, jumping from 100 to 256 in 2016, then to 512 and, soon after, to 1,024 in 2022.

Now, as spotted by WABetaInfo, WhatsApp is once again expanding that limit, raising the maximum number of participants in a group chat to 1,500.

According to the website, the new limit is rolling out to users on iOS and Android, though the rollout is gradual, meaning “not every account will see the higher limit immediately.”

WhatsApp is automatically updating existing groups to support the new limit. This means that admins do not need to take any action to unlock the higher capacity. As soon as the update becomes available to their accounts, their groups will support up to 1500 members. As a result, the update lets admins add up to 476 new members to their existing groups.

This rollout comes as WhatsApp has been working to make group chats easier to manage. Just last month, the company announced four new features, including the ability to pin messages indefinitely, share status updates within groups, filter conversations by mentions and replies, and share recent message history with new members after they join.

Management stated that the company implemented a headcount reduction to 640 employees to reach a target revenue of $400,000 per employee. The company reported that its strategy now focuses on expanding into the commercial solar and virtual power plant (VPP) markets to diversify beyond standard residential installations. Management confirmed that it has retained Deloitte to manage accounting processes and is working with audit firm BDO to address historical reporting deficiencies.

And now we're moving into 2 other states. This will give us an additive, much larger additive than our current TPO and it will cause us, I believe, to have very strong residential bookings in addition to the commercial stuff you saw with John Bergh. Thank you.

It won't take a penny out of your pocket. You have to start making payments after it's installed and turned on and those payments are in lieu of making your utility payments, and those payments will be smaller than utility payments. So nothing out of your pocket, you get solar and your monthly bill for power goes down. That is the TPO pitch. That's why it's been so successful.

It has replaced the old pitch, which give me a check and 5 years from now, your check will be paid back and you'll start making profit. So TPO is that pitch now, the new pitch, virtual power plant, a little bit of explanation. If I had personal control over the batteries in 100 houses, okay? Those batteries can put out kilowatts of power each. And if I had control and they're all connected to the grid, that's what we do. We connect things to the grid. So those batteries at Joe Blow's house can be run backwards and go into the grid.

And there's a measurement, utility quality, meaning monetary worthy measurement of how much power you put in the grid, you get paid for that. So how do you make money? So Joe Blow makes money because he buys battery, he absorbs power during the day. He puts power in his battery during the day and then he uses it at night. So this is an adder to that model. He now gets a bigger battery for no extra cost.

So instead of your average battery, which is 5 kilowatt hours, maybe 10, but it's really like 5, which is enough to back up your house and enough to give you power during the peak hours when the utilities charge more money. That is after 4:00 in the afternoon. You get a much bigger battery and you sign a deal that says, I got extra battery that I don't use, you have the right to use it and sell the power. So I then have a professional crew elsewhere aggregating my house and 50 other houses into a virtual power plant. And it's real simple.

They take in the power at noon when it's worth $0.05 a kilowatt hour, and they sell it at night in California or in San Diego, let's say, when it's worth $0.40 a kilowatt hour, there's arbitrage there. And that's how they make money. And because they're making money from another source, because of the extra size of the battery, price to make it attractive to the customer because they're making profit, they can afford to give a more liberal deal on the battery, battery size and the install because they're going to make the arbitrage money running the power. And then the contract they have with the customer is called the VPPA, Virtual Power Purchase Agreement.

And the customer says, I have a big battery, you have the right to use x amount of power from my battery. And in a typical day, that battery might get charged and discharged a couple of times to take advantage with professionals buying and selling power in a different market that none of us really understand that well. So the 2 vectors of growth to go away from the original SunPower only, $65 million a quarter, and we will make money at that level. We've done it before. We will do it again even with ITC. 2 growth vectors are commercial, big jobs, million-dollar jobs that are more profitable because you amortize overhead for obvious reasons.

And then virtual power plants where the vector is the strategy is to sell a bigger battery than the person needs and get the right to control it and therefore, to make money on the arbitrage and power. Those are the 2 ways we're going to grow beyond the simple residential model we inherited from SunPower. Okay. By the way, my solar airplane in case you have noticed got AI. That's actually a real picture of real airplane flying and it's been AI to get [indiscernible]. Questions?

Sioban Hickie: [Operator Instructions] Our first question today comes from Derek Soderberg from Cantor Fitzgerald.

Thurman Rodgers: Okay. First of all, right now, capital is not limiting us. The way the financial industry supporting solar works is I have to pay the sales force. First thing that happens, we say, okay, and we go through a process and we go through a process to buy what's required to put solar in the house, and we do that. We don't pay that.

Then we have the desk spot between finishing the job and going through two approvals. Thurman Rodgers: No, no. PTO. PTO, permission to operate, so turning on the power. So you get AHJ building commit and then you get utility permission, then the finisher turned on right away. And at that point, you get a third payment, which is small. Typically, it's like 10% to 20% of the job. So in order to attract customers and reap 30% benefit, the ITC is not dead for these. They still get it. It's for individual companies and individuals. The ITC benefit was a benefit to individual homeowners that refunded on their next tax submission, 30% of any job they did. That's gone.

So the little guy doesn't get the benefit anymore, but the big guys, the money guys behind the solar industry got taken care of. So right now, there is no capital limitation on growth. Our limitation on growth is we're $300 million, $280 million company. We've got 640 people, and we have to make the machine run faster. It's not about dollars coming into the machine. #3253. Microsoft will pay top Azure staff more and get tougher on the rest

A memo from Azure's boss says pay will track performance more closely as AI competition heats up.

Microsoft’s office in Dubai Internet City, Dubai, 3 November 2026

Microsoft is making pay in its Azure cloud division more performance-based, with extra stock awards for top performers and formal meetings with managers for those with lower results, Bloomberg reported, citing a memo from Azure chief Arun Ulagaratchagan.

Microsoft will tie pay in its Azure cloud unit more closely to how well staff do, Bloomberg reported on Friday. Top performers will get extra stock. Staff with weaker results will face formal meetings with their bosses.

The plan was set out in a memo from Arun Ulagaratchagan, who runs Azure. Bloomberg has seen the memo.

“Pay-for-performance only works if we are equally rigorous on both sides: recognizing exceptional impact and being honest when performance falls short,” Ulagaratchagan wrote.

He told staff that meeting today’s bar means closing past gaps and showing “a meaningful step-change in impact.” AI is reshaping how the world works, he said, and the competition has never been tougher.

A Microsoft spokesperson confirmed the change, saying it brings “meaningful additional awards” for the best performers. Staff will also get clearer goals and more direct feedback from their bosses, the spokesperson said.

Azure sales grew 48% last quarter, but the unit is also under cost pressure. In October, an Azure executive reportedly asked teams to find 20% cost cuts, partly to fund higher pay. Microsoft disputed that report.

Last month, Microsoft offered buyouts to about 60,000 employees, around a quarter of its staff. A pay spreadsheet built by staff showed the largest stock awards already going to Cloud and AI workers.

Other tech giants are pushing staff harder too. Google has offered voluntary buyouts in more countries. Its workers’ union wants it to stop rating staff on a curve.

#3252. Community-Focused Academic Brings AI Tools to Colorado Farmers

This senior member’s chatbot helps them start agritourism businesses

Willie Jones covers transportation for IEEE Spectrum and the history of technology for The Institute.

Alice Dong has created an AI chatbot website that helps Colorado farmers plan and operate agribusinesses that draw visitors to their properties.

Many farmers and ranchers in eastern Colorado are curious about artificial intelligence, but they don’t have a local tech-savvy person to show them how to use it. Xue “Alice” Dong has made that her job.

Dong, an IEEE senior member, is an extension regional specialist with the Colorado State University Extension, CSU’s outreach arm. She works in Logan County and serves a 10-county farming area in Colorado’s northeast corner. Her job is to turn university research into practical help for the people who live there.

Xue “Alice” Dong Employer Colorado State University Extension in Logan CountyTitle Extension regional specialistMember grade Senior memberAlma maters Inner Mongolia Normal University, in Hohhot; Beijing Normal University; State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry, in Syracuse; Colorado State University Global

Colorado State University Extension in Logan County

Inner Mongolia Normal University, in Hohhot; Beijing Normal University; State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry, in Syracuse; Colorado State University Global

She built the AI-Powered Agritourism Chatbot (AgriTourismAI.com), which helps farmers and ranchers launch and run “agritourism” businesses. Agritourism is when farmers open their property to visitors for fun, education, or shopping events. Familiar examples include pick-your-own fruit orchards, lessons on how to grow vegetables, and sales of handmade products.

Dong also teaches workshops where she shows farmers and ranchers how they can use AI tools to help grow and manage their business.

She says she sees herself as a link between the university and the countryside.

“We [extension specialists] act as a bridge,” she says. “We bridge our campus to the rural communities we serve.”

Many farmers and ranchers are older, and they typically have no technical training. Often their children and grandchildren have left the farm to work in a city or otherwise aren’t around to teach them about new tools. Without help, the benefits of AI could pass the farmers by. Dong’s workshops give them a way in.

Dong was named a finalist in the 2026 GenAI for Good Challenge for her AgriPivot AI Agent. The challenge was organized by IEEE Humanitarian Technologies and theU.N.’s International Telecommunication Union, and her project was selected from 318 teams across 79 countries. She also won the 2026 Award for Innovation from the National Extension Technology Community (NETC), and both the 2025 national and Western regional Educational Technology Awards from the National Association of Community Development Extension Professionals (NACDEP).

She has secured seven competitive grants totaling more than US $250,000 as principal investigator or co-principal investigator, including funding supported by the Department of Agriculture’s National Institute of Food and Agriculture.

Dong was born in Beijing. Both her parents are doctors.

As a child, she liked drawing new and inventive things. Sketching, she says, lets her picture solutions to problems in her head and put them on paper as practical designs.

That habit grew into a way of relating to her surroundings.

“I’ve always had a passion to create something tangible that can solve problems in the real world,” she says.

She doesn’t credit a single mentor for the direction her life has taken. Instead, she says all her teachers helped lay the groundwork for her career.

She attended the Inner Mongolia Normal University, in Hohhot, an institution that trains teachers. She earned two bachelor’s degrees there in 2013—one in geographical science and one in education.

She then earned a master’s degree in curriculum and instruction from Beijing Normal University in 2016.

That year, she moved to the United States to continue her graduate studies at the State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry, in Syracuse. She earned a master’s degree in environmental biology in 2020.

After earning her second master’s degree, she joined Paul Smith’s College, in Paul Smiths, N.Y., as an education and outreach coordinator.

She managed several national watershed projects to protect rivers, lakes, and aquifers. Watersheds are areas of land from which water drains into bodies of water.

She also undertook invasive-species-prevention projects, wrote grants to secure project funding, and designed two educational websites and several outreach publications. One website, Maintain the Chain, helps lake residents, boaters, and visitors from around the world keep invasive species out of the Fulton Chain of Lakes in New York’s Adirondack Park.

In 2022, she joined Stewards of the Coast and Redwoods as program manager. The nonprofit, based in Guerneville, Calif., works with California State Parks to protect, restore, and educate the public about the parks along Sonoma County’s coast and the Russian River area. The region is known for its redwood forests, wineries, and resort towns.

She left in 2023 to join the CSU Extension as a regional specialist, a title she still holds.

Her employer is part of the Cooperative Extension System, a nationwide network run by land-grant universities, schools founded with federal grants to teach farming and other practical subjects. Extension faculty and staff share what researchers at their universities learn with the citizens of those states.

The cooperative system operates on three levels. It is overseen federally by the Department of Agriculture’s National Institute of Food and Agriculture, managed statewide through land-grant universities, and delivered locally by county offices and Extension agents across more than 3,000 counties.

The work goes well beyond farming, Dong says, also covering community and economic development, health initiatives, and the 4-H program, which teaches children hands-on skills in agriculture, science, leadership, and citizenship.

Extension faculty members’ performance is judged on their research, teaching, and service to the community, Dong says—similar to the way professors in academia are evaluated. The difference, she says, is the audience: Professors teach students; most extension specialists teach adults, including farmers, ranchers, and community leaders. The setting is different, too. Dong doesn’t commute from the campus to the countryside; she lives and works in it. Her office is in Sterling, a small rural town. But her projects serve the whole state, and many of the people she helps live one to four hours’ drive away. So, most of her work with farmers and ranchers happens by email, phone, and virtual meetings. County fairs, farmers markets, and agricultural events give her chances to meet large groups of them in person.

She can’t just hand Colorado residents research findings and expect them to figure out the information they need, she says.

“We need to translate that research into something more practical, and easier to use, that farmers and ranchers can understand immediately,” she says.

Dong also focuses not on only on whether people use AI, but also on how they use it. In 2026, she and Paul Hill from Utah State University Extension published “From Access to Governance: Generative AI Literacy for Extension Professionals and Small Businesses, and a Governance-Aware Design Framework” in the journal AI. The paper offers a framework for helping Extension professionals and small businesses adopt generative AI responsibly.

In 2025, Dong earned a third master’s degree, in artificial intelligence and machine learning, from CSU Global.

She immediately put those skills to work on agritourism, she says. She built the chatbot in Python, a popular programming language. It answers typed questions, and its user interface looks much like ChatGPT’s, but it works differently. Under the hood, it uses retrieval-augmented generation, a technique that has the AI look up information in a set of trusted documents before it answers. Dong curated that collection from Extension publications, so the chatbot’s answers rest on authoritative sources and are less likely to be made up. She presented the project at NeurIPS 2025 (Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems). The code is openly available on GitHub, so other Extension offices can adapt it.

The bot runs in a web browser rather than as a phone app. Many farmers she works with don’t own a smartphone, Dong says, but nearly all have a computer, tablet, or other gadget that can connect to a website. The bot works on any of them, with no app to download.

Extension specialists “act as a bridge. We bridge our campus to the rural communities we serve.”

Farmers often ask the bot how to attract visitors and how to write a business plan. A farmer thinking about opening a corn maze, for example, can ask how to price admission, what kind of insurance to carry, and which permits to get. The bot also gives advice on managing risk.

One of her test sites was Prairie Ridge Buffalo Ranch, in eastern Colorado. Dong documented how the ranch put AI to work in a peer-reviewed case study, “Revolutionizing Agritourism with AI and Machine Learning: A Case Study of Prairie Ridge Buffalo Ranch in Colorado,” published in 2025 in CABI Tourism Cases.

Surveys and interviews she conducted with other users showed that people find it’s easy to use the bot, learn from it, and act on its advice, she says. She is preparing the full results for publication.

Her work extends beyond agritourism. In 2026, she contributed an AI assistant to Project Pythia, an open-science program funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation and led by the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR). The AI assistant turns raw airport weather report data into plain-language guidance for farmers and other non-technical users, and it tells users when data is missing rather than guessing.

She also teaches workshops on AI tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. She has taught her workshop 20 times to more than 200 entrepreneurs and business owners, who came from 32 Colorado counties. In follow-up surveys, 90 percent of participants reported trying at least one new AI task in their business. Some of the workshops take place at a community center run by the Logan County Economic Development Corp., in Sterling. She has also co-hosted the workshops with the Rural Community Assistance Corp., Colorado Startup Week, and Boulder Startup Week. And she occasionally presents them as webinars, so people don’t have to travel.

Her outreach has taught her that many farmers are eager to try new tools, she says. She shows them how simple her chatbot is to use.

She also offers advice to high school students drawn to the field. Extension specialists each have a specialty, such as livestock, natural resources, food systems, or 4-H. Students should pick one based on their passion, she says.

Land-grant universities offer related programs at the bachelor’s and master’s levels. For graduate students, she adds, Extension offers a third career path beyond academia and industry: “You apply advanced skills directly to the communities that need them.”

Dong joined IEEE in 2025 and soon was elevated to senior member. Her professional home is the IEEE Society on Social Implications of Technology. She also serves as vice treasurer of the IEEE Denver Section’s Young Professionals group.

IEEE supports all three parts of her job, she says. For research, she presented “Entrepreneur AI Agent: Empowering Small Businesses and Bridging the Digital Divide through Context-Aware Generative AI” at the 2026 IEEE Global Humanitarian Technology Conference (GHTC). For teaching, she has offered to bring her AI workshop to Denver Section members and local entrepreneurs. For service, she reviews papers for IEEE conferences.

IEEE conferences matter most to her, she says: “Through them, I can present my research and network with other researchers in the field.”

She attended the IEEE World Forum on Public Safety Technology in Boulder, Colo., in September 2026. The event, she says, opened her eyes to many new projects underway across IEEE.

Still, she says, her work always points back to the farms and ranches of eastern Colorado. Its people are curious, she says, but they can’t make the leap to new technology alone.

“They really need this kind of a bridge,” she says.

Willie Jones is an associate editor at IEEE Spectrum. In addition to editing and planning daily coverage, he manages several of Spectrum's newsletters and contributes regularly to the monthly Big Picture section that appears in the print edition.

The makers behind Assassin’s Creed are going all in on generative AI while letting human talent go

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Every time news comes out about the French video game publisher/developer Ubisoft, it’s either something gamers are pleasantly surprised by or something entirely negative that doesn’t come as a shock.

It was nice to learn that studio franchises like Assassin’s Creed, The Division and Rayman were either getting content expansions or new series installments altogether. But it was equally disappointing to learn about the 2026 cancellation of several in-development projects, including the troubled remake of Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time. Gamers were ecstatic to hear that Ubisoft halted any future development in NFTs and Web3 gaming. But now they’ll probably be less than enthused all over again, now that Ubisoft is shifting its next big tech focus to generative AI.

After releasing its latest earnings report, Ubisoft has announced its intentions to go all-in on incorporating generative AI technologies into video game development with a new studio. But with that news comes the company’s latest round of layoffs, which resulted in hundreds of its studio’s game developers losing their roles at Ubisoft.

With both events happening so close to each other, it’s easy to see why gamers are questioning Ubisoft’s latest moves.

Ubisoft made it known that they’re making a big move towards playable generative AI experiences when it highlighted the new in-house studio behind its efforts in its most recent earnings report.

“Motherbrain, the team behind Teammates, the Group’s first playable generative AI experience, has been established as a dedicated subsidiary developing proprietary technology for new forms of gameplay. Its current focus is on new player experiences, smart NPCs with memory and AI game masters that manage large-scale systemic worlds,” the company stated. “It aims to serve creators globally, both within Ubisoft’s Creative House ecosystem and beyond, and form partnerships with selected technology actors.”

Ubisoft CEO Yves Guillemot commented on the creation of Motherbrain, noting that it is “the team behind our first playable generative AI experience Teammates, as a dedicated subsidiary developing proprietary technologies for gameplay to empower creators and open up new possibilities for richer, more immersive and engaging player experiences.”

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

Those experiences will focus on utilizing more intelligent non-playable characters with stronger memory and AI game masters that properly manage large-scale in-game worlds.

Motherbrain’s Teammates has been in development for a good while now and was recently showcased to members of the gaming media in a playable state. The people who got their hands on it refer to it as an immersive first-person shooter where players are joined by two robotic AI companions that they can order around by issuing real-time voice commands.

The game’s narrative director, Virginie Mosser, looked to ease the fears of gamers who are wary of generative AI being implemented in video games and AI tools being used to make them.

“At first, I had the same concerns as many others,” Mosser noted. “But I discovered that it’s the exact opposite of removing the human from the process. I still write the story and character personalities, but instead of fixed lines, we create these kinds of fences that let NPCs improvise within the world but stay within the boundaries of the lore and motivations we have given them. They can improvise, but we still set the rules and direct the story and characters.”

Gamers still have reason to give Ubisoft the side eye about its big generative AI video game development plans, especially since the company was so quick to abandon its trend-chasing foray into the world of NFTs and Web3 gaming. The most recent round of layoffs at the company, which resulted in the loss of 166 roles from its Montreal and Quebec studios, has also given gamers another reason to be skeptical about Ubisoft’s AI game-making initiative.

Even though Ubisoft enacted these layoffs “to ensure our resources are aligned with current production priorities and business needs,” it’s not out of the realm of possibility to question its true motives for its latest job cuts.

Has Ubisoft decided to pour major investments into generative AI game development at the cost of sacrificing its human talent? Will more layoffs occur in the near future as the company strengthens its AI game development efforts? Can gamers expect to hear about more AI tool usage implemented in the creation of future entries in Ubisoft’s biggest franchises? And if Motherbrain’s Teammates bombs, will Ubisoft quickly leave generative AI video game development behind and go on to the next big tech fad?

As someone who’s always chatting with gamers and critics who cover the medium, I always hear how they could do without any sort of AI being utilized in the video game creation process. And they especially don’t want to hear AI voices emanating from their favorite games and replacing human ones.

That last sentiment is evidenced by the overwhelmingly negative reactions to Embark Studios (the development studio behind The Finals) replacing its human esports broadcasters with in-game AI commentators. Ubisoft has experienced some major ups and downs as of late—their major bet on generative AI game development has a high chance of producing another loss if their latest endeavors don’t work as well as intended.

We'll start with Brent Hinds going over the company financials for the third quarter of 2026. Brent?

For the third quarter of 2026, the company recognized approximately $712,000 in revenues compared to approximately $1 million for the same period in 2025. The year-over-year decrease in revenue was primarily attributable to product mix. While the product mix during the quarter resulted in lower reported revenue, it generated meaningful improvement in gross margins.

As discussed in our Q2 conference call, we entered into a licensing arrangement with an OEM heater manufacturer to build 3 M Series midstream burners, and we successfully fulfilled our obligations under this arrangement during the third quarter of 2026. Our third quarter gross profit margin was approximately 55.6%, which is an increase of almost 20 percentage points over the prior comparable period's margin of 35.8%. This year-over-year improvement in gross margin was primarily driven by our licensing arrangement with an OEM heater manufacturer. We believe licensing arrangements like this further diversifies our go-to-market strategy and we expect to continue pursuing such arrangements to further expand our revenue channels.

We also believe licensing arrangements like this will bolster our overall gross margin and help us achieve our overall long-term company gross margin target of 40%. Now moving on to the full P&L. Our net loss for the third quarter decreased by $361,000 compared to the same period in 2025. The decrease in our net loss was predominantly driven by a $601,000 decrease in general and administrative expenses, offset by a $233,000 decrease in other income. Our G&A expenses decreased predominantly due to a one-time noncash expense in the prior period related to the vesting of restricted stock units issued to our former Directors. Other income decreased predominantly because our Department of Energy grant completed in May of 2026.

Now let's shift our focus to cash. Our net cash used in operations for the third quarter of 2026 was approximately $1.3 million compared to approximately $1.8 million for the same period in 2025. This improvement was driven predominantly by timing of customer cash collections. As of September 30, 2026, we had approximately $10.3 million in cash and cash equivalents. As of September 30, 2026, we had approximately 6.8 million shares of common stock outstanding. And with that, I'd like to turn the call over to Matthew Selinger.

Matthew Selinger: Brent, thank you for the financial overview. And Colin, thank you for joining me today here. I'd like to start the call with a brief overview of ClearSign, Colin, what we do, how we do it for any new investors. After that, I think we'll dive into the product lines and company developments. So with that, Colin, could you summarize briefly for a high level, what does ClearSign do?

Colin James Deller: Yes, certainly. So really high level, right? We have unique IP and some leading engineers with the company. So our clients are large oil refineries, petrochemical companies, midstream gas companies, generally companies in the energy business, right? As part of their production, they burn fuel gases, right, natural gas or gas blends, to make their process work, whether it's heating up oil to break it down or whatever. As part of that combustion process, they make toxic gases and we're primarily concerned with NOx emissions. These are nitrogen oxides. These gases are highly regulated.

They have to operate within them to stay within their permits. They're controlled by the local air regulators. And the traditional technology that allows them to get down to the latest levels we're seeing in California and Texas is they call a selective catalytic reduction unit. This is a very expensive piece of equipment that has to be built into the back end of the heaters and then it has to be supplied with ammonia to operate. With our unique technology, we can provide special burners that essentially do not make the NOx emissions in the first place. So you might be -- we've all had kids.

It's also one of the benefits of product lines like the midstream burners in this case, where we have standard products and we have clients that have the ability to manufacture their own burners. What's special to ClearSign is the IP and the designs. So in this case, we are able to provide the fabrication drawings to the client on a licensing basis to give them the ability to fabricate their own burners.

For ClearSign, we make exactly the same profit, whether it's a license sale or whether we are supplying the equipment. Of course, so the -- it's really been a win-win. The burners the client manufactured look fantastic. I actually got to see them myself. We also put some photographs on LinkedIn. Sameer Joshi: Should we expect, or let me ask it this way, are there other and more customers who are looking at this model? Or is it only this one customer that is looking to manufacture it themselves?

Sameer Joshi: Understood. And then moving on to the M Series, I think it was mentioned that you had 5 orders in 3Q and 2 orders in 4Q so far. And one of the -- what actually makes these questions hard to answer specifically is we have orders coming in that we have not specifically quoted, but we have sufficient -- we've given our customers sufficient details of our standard burners that match their standard heaters. Sameer Joshi: And just one last one maybe for Brent and maybe I missed it in the commentary, but in addition to operating expenses being lower year-over-year, they were lower sequentially as well. So was there an explanation given for the sequentially lower OpEx?

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Your next question is coming from Peter Gastreich from Water Tower Research.

Peter Gastreich: Congratulations on the quarter. It's good to hear the Gulf Coast burners are up and running, and nice to see the M1 orders keep coming in. So it's a single-burner heater. There's a lot of engineering involved in the order. I don't have the specific numbers to hand, but it's in the range of $500,000 to $750,000 from memory. Colin James Deller: So you asked about the timing and I'll tell you my expectations. We've completed the contractual details which involve the other representative of the DOE. We still have to work out the exact schedule with Kern. My expectations are that we will receive the order from them early Q1. I do believe that they're still completing permits, so that is a caveat on that statement. With that, my best guess will be to complete the order somewhere around late Q3, early Q4 next year. Again, those are estimates on my part. We've not worked out those details yet, so they may change. But that's my expectation for the progression of that project.

Peter Gastreich: Okay, great, thank you. So most of my detailed questions that I had in mind have been answered, and I appreciate that. So I just have a couple of bigger picture questions for you. So your team has talked about burners that improve yield and uptime, not just cut the emissions. So are there customers that are just generally starting to see ClearSign as a way to improve plant profitability? And could that open additional markets that aren't necessarily driven purely by NOx rules? Or is that not the right way to look at it?

Colin James Deller: No, that, Peter, is exactly the right way to look at those opportunities. And really what's exciting is if we can improve the yield or improve the uptime for a client, we're no longer just a cost for compliance with emissions, we actually give them a significant return on their investment. The Texas project that is currently on hold, unfortunately, was actually based on improving the uptime of that furnace as one of the primary drivers. So that was one project that's been through the engineering, we completed the CFD modeling, and we're able to demonstrate those benefits to the customer at that phase. So it's -- yes, it is something we're pursuing.

It's something we've been able to demonstrate to our client. And going forward, as we're able to show more and more to the industry what we can do, my expectation is that we will be able to capitalize on that ability to a greater extent.

Peter Gastreich: Okay. And just a final question. So your CTO, Matt Martin, he mentioned on our podcast a little bit ago that the M Series and the flare design went straight from computer modeling to the field. I just want to ask, how does that change the cost and speed of bringing new products to market and where does AI kind of fit in with ClearSign?

Colin James Deller: First question's easy. The ability to design a burner in CFD to the extent that we can create fabrication drawings and send it out to the field and have the success we've had on the M1 burner is a game changer. It typically takes probably an additional 6 months to a year when you're going through the slow process of optimizing a burner in a test furnace, and then you have to wait for mechanical changes to be made and then fire it up. In the computer, you can check out different ideas. You can see what's going on inside the burner and inside the flames.

And then rather than speculating what changes you need to make, you can actually see what's going on and make surgical changes to optimize the process. So the -- anyone doesn't know this, the very first M1 burner was drawn from the output from our computer modeling program. It was put in a heater, and that design has never been touched. And that burner has actually demonstrated NOx down below 2 ppm. It is still out there running today and is the benchmark for our entire M1 product line. So this is one of the -- I'm just going to brag a little bit on our CTO, Matthew Martin, the resources here at ClearSign.

We've been able to develop the computer modeling technology for combustion systems and burners, I believe, to the greatest extent anywhere in the world in my opinion, and that has allowed us to bring technologies like this to market in the speed that we have and to actually put them out in the field and have the success we've had both with the flare and the M Series. But to answer your basic question, it is hugely significant for ClearSign and the speed that we can bring not only new technologies, but also adapt technologies for specific client needs and show them how those products will work modeled inside their furnace as part of our sales or project validation process.

Peter Gastreich: Great. And congratulations.

Colin James Deller: I appreciate your questions, Peter. Thank you.

They are -- above everything else, they are waiting to see the technology running in somebody else's heater. So yes, the simple answer to that is yes, we believe so. We are just excited to be able to get out and talk about it.

Matthew Selinger: And Colin, in the past, the company, you have stated a kind of a break-even number of 160 burners a year. Do you believe that is obtainable potentially next year? Or is that a further target? What are your thoughts there?

Colin James Deller: Yes. That number was based on $100,000 per year, so $16 million run rate, right? The math works out to get the company to break even. We absolutely have the line of sight in the pipeline to get to that number. I mean, it is 3 or 4 process burner orders, a couple of flares, and then the runway with the M Series. It's a very pragmatic expectation for the company. That's the one question we can't guarantee is just the timing, right? But yes, the loads out there, the opportunities are definitely out there.

Matthew Selinger: With that, Colin, there are no more questions. So with that, I will hand the call back to you if you'd like any closing statements.

Colin James Deller: Great. Thank you very much. Thank you, everyone. I really appreciate you tuning in to this call and for your interest in ClearSign, especially taking your time and giving us your time this afternoon. We look forward to updating you regarding our developments and speaking with you on our Q4 and full year call in April next year. We don't plan on being quiet with news on them. So please continue to check in on the websites. We do encourage you to follow us on LinkedIn. Of course, when we have a significant announcement, we will be putting press releases out in addition to that. So thank you very much.

Operator: Thank you everyone. This concludes today's event. You may disconnect at this time and have a wonderful day. Thank you for your participation.

#3247. I Don’t Trust Visual Recordings Anymore. But One Day I Will Again

We will have to label our content to prove its authenticity

Hany Farid is a computer science professor at Dartmouth College, in Hanover, N.H.

In March of this year, a flurry of emails and text messages from a half dozen reporters around the world disrupted my quiet Saturday morning. An Iranian news agency had aired a week-old video of what appeared to be a U.S.-made Tomahawk missile hitting a school. News reports claimed that the strike killed more than 175 people, most of them children. The U.S. president and military denied responsibility. In the age of generative AI and all things deepfake, everyone—including me—was skeptical of the video’s authenticity.

I get this type of request a lot. For the past three decades, I’ve been developing mathematical and computational techniques to analyze and detect manipulation in digital media. Over this time, I think it’s fair to say that I, like most people, have approached visual recordings with a “presumption of authenticity”: If a skeptic claims that a recording is fake, the burden of proof is on them.

In today’s world of generative AI, however, I think we need to shift this stance to a “presumption of fake.” That is, the burden is now on the creator to prove that their content is real. While this new stance may seem unfair to legitimate creators, I think it both reflects reality and points to a future where we will once again be able to trust that most online media is what it appears to be.

Even last March, I was already tilting toward a presumption of fake. My initial response to the reporters was something along the lines of, “I am suspicious of the video because the quality is low, it emerged weeks after the bombing, and it is only being distributed by an Iranian news agency with a less-than-stellar record of accurate reporting.”

Given the potential implications—if the video was indeed real, however, I resigned myself to spending my Saturday morning analyzing it.

I first reasoned that if the Tomahawk missile was digitally added to each frame of the video without taking into consideration the camera motion, we might see a physically implausible missile path. So I aligned the video frames using a stationary background landmark as a reference. In the updated video, the missile did, in fact, move in a nearly linear trajectory. (See the yellow dots in the composite shown below.)

I next asked if the size (in pixels) of the missile in the video was plausible. Under some reasonable assumptions, I estimated that the missile in the video corresponded to a 6-meter Tomahawk at a distance of approximately 100 meters. The distance seemed plausible from the scene and was also consistent with the delay of 0.3 seconds from visible impact to the sound of impact, given that sound travels at 343 meters per second.

A composite photo composed of frames from a video of the Tomahawk strike reveals the missile’s trajectory.Hany Farid; Source: Mehr News

Despite the mounting evidence, though, I struggled to refine my answer for the reporters.

My skepticism was fueled by a recent study I worked on with colleagues at the University of California, Berkeley, that showed how hard it is to distinguish real from fake videos. Observers are now so suspicious of videos in general that they have trouble convincing themselves that a video is real.

But after a few more hours and a few more analyses with the missile video, I finally decided that it was authentic, and I gave the reporters my updated view.

This analysis marked a turning point for me. I realized I was just like the participants in our study: The lack of artifacts was not enough to readily convince me a video is real. I had flipped from a presumption of real to a presumption of fake.

When the visual record is no longer reliable, what can we do?

The types of forensic analyses that I routinely perform do not currently operate at internet scale and speed. But provenance signals can. These signals include content credentials and watermarks that are inserted or embedded at the time of creation or recording.

Credentials that follow the C2PA standard, for example, attach a cryptographically signed manifest to a photo or video at the moment of capture; this metadata records the device, the time and location of the recording, and any subsequent edits. Because the manifest is signed, any tampering with either the content or its history can be detected later by machine. Watermarks, like Google’s SynthID, embed an imperceptible signal directly into the pixels or audio samples that identifies the content’s origin.

Apple recently took these ideas a step further. On some of its newest iPhones, the camera sensor can cryptographically sign the raw pixel data as it’s captured. That signed data is then developed into a reference image saved alongside the normal, editable photo. Anyone can then compare the two and see exactly what, if anything, was changed.

These provenance signals are often criticized as being only a partial solution or vulnerable to attack. This is true if we think of them as mechanisms for catching bad actors. But that’s not what they’re supposed to do. Their purpose is to let good actors prove that their audiovisual recording is what it claims to be.

Provenance signals thus need not be adversary-proof. Instead, these signals are part of a new reality in which consumers, journalists, and the courts must adapt to a presumption of fakeness. If enough good actors adopt these mechanisms, they can begin to drown out bad actors. In other words, we have to switch from a model of “catch the bad actors” to “empower the good actors.”

This switch from trust to distrust of digital media has expanded to include routine video calls.

In September 2024, for example, Senator Ben Cardin (D-Md.), then chair of the Foreign Relations Committee, received a video meeting request from Dmytro Kuleba, who until a few weeks earlier had been Ukraine’s foreign minister. During the call, Cardin became suspicious when, out of character, Kuleba pressed him on whether the U.S. should allow Ukraine to fire long-range missiles into Russia. Cardin ended the call. Later, the State Department confirmed that Kuleba had never requested the meeting, and the Senate security office warned staff that foreign adversaries, possibly Russian, would likely try similar faked meetings again.

All it takes to conduct this type of impersonation is a face swap or avatar deepfake, along with voice conversion, both of which substitute the speaker’s face and voice for deepfaked versions in real time. These technologies are readily available in commercial products and open-source libraries and run on nothing more powerful than a modern laptop.

This video illustrates the current state of face-swap deepfakes.

Farid’s Company GetReal Shows How Real Deepfake Videos Look Today Your browser does not support the video tag. Firms that verify provenance have to move fast to detect real-time deepfakes. Hany Farid, GetReal

Firms that verify provenance have to move fast to detect real-time deepfakes. Hany Farid, GetReal

Unlike the Tomahawk video, which I could sit with for a morning analyzing frame by frame, a live video call offers no time for human analysis. On the other hand, real-time deepfakes pose new challenges for their creators: A fake video call has to be generated at around 24 frames per second to fool the eye into perceiving realistic motion. As a result, the deepfake-video-call software has to take shortcuts, such as simplifying faces and how they interact with their surroundings, and allowing some drift between audio and video or between video frames. The human eye doesn’t notice the shortcuts, but we can forensically expose them.

Provenance signals should eventually play a role here. Video-calling software could apply the same cryptographic signing to each frame of a live video stream that Apple now applies to still photographs. A face swap necessarily occurs between a speaker’s camera and the videoconferencing software, and so the software could verify in real time whether the frames it’s receiving were signed by a physical camera sensor or whether they were altered in transit. As before, the burden shifts from catching the impersonator to allowing real participants to prove they are who they claim to be.

For the first two decades of the digital revolution, forensic analysis—finding the telltale traces of manipulation—was enough to adjudicate most questions of authenticity. The AI revolution, however, has changed the scale and speed of manipulation beyond what forensics alone can handle. To believe a recording is real now, it must also carry a provenance signal from the point of recording. The two approaches work together, with provenance allowing good actors to be trusted, while forensic analyses root out the bad actors.

Hany Farid is a computer science professor at Dartmouth College, in Hanover, N.H. About 10 years ago, he randomly picked up a book in the library on the federal rules of evidence and was astonished to learn that courts made no distinction between photos from negatives and digital photos, even though the latter can be easily altered. “Digital photography was just getting started,” Farid says. “I realized this was really going to be a huge problem.” Since then digital photo forensics has become the focus of his research. He now frequently testifies in U.S. courts and advises law enforcement agencies. “All that from picking up a book,” he says.

The emerging authentication and provenance systems make a lot of sense for mainstream uses. I get the impression we'll still need forensic analysis for plenty of edge cases, though. People using older hardware or anyone trying to capture evidence in situations where it isn't safe to share clues about the media's origin come to mind.

#3246. Ripple Is Rapidly Expanding the Potential Use Cases for Its Stablecoin. Here's Why That's Bearish for XRP.

Don't expect XRP to share in Ripple USD's success.

By Lyle Daly – Nov 20, 2026 at 11:30AM EST

Ripple had a big week in late October, striking deals with Robinhood and Coinbase to support its stablecoin, Ripple USD (RLUSD +0.02%). The blockchain company is also the largest holder of XRP (XRP -7.41%), and CEO Brad Garlinghouse has said that XRP and stablecoins like Ripple USD are complementary rather than competitive.

With that in mind, Ripple USD's success may seem like good news for XRP. I'm not convinced; these deals look more like XRP getting left behind.

On Oct. 27, Robinhood announced Ripple USD was live on Robinhood Chain and Bitstamp, the cryptocurrency exchange it acquired last year. It will be available in the Robinhood app later this year. Robinhood will use Ripple USD on the XRP Ledger (XRPL) to settle institutional trades on Bitstamp, and it will integrate Ripple Treasury into its global treasury operations.

A day later, Ripple and Coinbase announced a partnership, with the crypto exchange making Ripple USD available on Coinbase Prime, Coinbase Exchange, and the Coinbase Retail app. Coinbase Global Exchange customers will eventually be able to use the stablecoin as collateral.

The problem for XRP holders is that Ripple USD isn't reliant on the cryptocurrency or its blockchain. About 74% of the Ripple USD supply is on Ethereum, according to DeFiLlama data from Nov. 19, compared to 25% on the XRPL and the rest on other blockchains. Coinbase's stablecoin integration supports Ethereum, Base, and XRPL.

In fairness, there's still a sizable amount of Ripple USD on the XRPL, and it's nearly 90% of the blockchain's total stablecoin supply. XRP is the native cryptocurrency on the XRPL and is used to pay transaction fees. However, this is where the network's low fees can be a double-edged sword. Transaction fees start at 0.00001 XRP, meaning even Ripple USD activity doesn't generate much demand for XRP.

An even deeper issue is that Ripple USD cannibalizes XRP's primary use case. The pitch for XRP is that it can serve as a bridge currency for financial institutions to send and receive cross-border payments. But a stablecoin pegged at $1 works much better as a bridge currency than a volatile cryptocurrency like XRP. The more Ripple USD grows, the less XRP is needed.

Ripple USD is having a successful 2026, going from a market cap of $1.3 billion at the start of the year to $2.8 billion as of Nov. 18, becoming one of the 10 largest stablecoins in the process. XRP, on the other hand, has plummeted from a market cap of $122 billion in January to $63 billion. Institutional demand has fallen, with spot XRP ETFs losing $19.1 million in the week ending Nov. 13, the largest weekly outflow in eight months.

The partnerships with Robinhood and Coinbase show that Ripple is building a legitimate stablecoin business. That's good for Ripple and Ripple USD, but the success doesn't flow back to XRP.

#3245. iPhone Air 2 dummy unit shows off new dual-camera design

Apple is expected to release the iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2 sometime next spring. Ahead of that launch, new dummy units posted to social media today give us a closer look at the devices, including a big update to the iPhone Air 2.

9to5Mac is supported by Sony: Score Sony’s ULT Field 1 Bluetooth speaker for 51% off. Powerful bass, room-filling sound, up to 12 hours of battery life, IP67 durability, stereo pairing support, and much more.

In a post on X, Sonny Dickson shared dummy units of the iPhone Air 2, giving us a glimpse of the new dual-camera system. Meanwhile, the base iPhone 18 looks largely unchanged compared to the iPhone 17.

The first-generation iPhone Air has a single 48MP Main camera. The second-generation model, however, will reportedly add an Ultra Wide camera.

First look at the iPhone 18 Air and iPhone 18 dummy units. The biggest change is the iPhone 18 Air, which now features two rear cameras instead of one, while the standard iPhone 18 retains a design similar to the iPhone 17. pic.twitter.com/MdOVuwPlm3

As expected, the iPhone Air 2 cameras are arranged horizontally across the pill-shaped camera plateau, similar to the iPhone Duo’s arrangement.

In addition to the dual-camera system, the iPhone Air 2 is expected to be powered by the A20 Pro chip. Apple is also reportedly working to improve the battery life. The Information has reported the device will feature a vapor chamber cooling system, which Apple debuted with the iPhone 17 Pro. Another report suggested the device will have a smaller Dynamic Island.

The base model iPhone 18, meanwhile, will reportedly use Apple’s A20 chip. Ming-Chi Kuo has reported it will have 9GB of RAM, up from the iPhone 17’s 8GB. It’s expected to be a modest year-over-year update, with Apple focused on cutting costs.

#3243. Lockheed Martin vs. SpaceX: Which Aerospace Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Defense giant or disruptive rocket leader: one carries federal backing and steady profits, the other a fast-growing satellite business still posting heavy losses.

By Brendan Coffey – Updated Nov 20, 2026 at 11:30AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Lockheed Martin ›

As space exploration needs evolve, investors often weigh defense stability against rapid disruption. Choosing between Lockheed Martin (LMT -0.87%) and Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX -6.66%) depends on your appetite for risk versus consistent performance.

Lockheed Martin serves as a cornerstone of national security by providing advanced aircraft and missile systems to global governments. Space Exploration Technologies--SpaceX-- focuses on reusable rockets and global satellite internet through its Starlink program. Both companies are central to the future of aerospace, making them a natural match-up for long-term retail investors.

In its latest annual report, filed for the most recent period, Lockheed Martin highlights its role as a premier global security company. It relies heavily on government contracts, with nearly 72% of its 2025 sales coming from agencies of the U.S. federal government. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business, as revenue depends on federal budget priorities.

Reliable recent quarterly figures for at least one of these companies aren't available, so this comparison uses each company's latest full fiscal year. In FY 2025, the company reported revenue of about $75.1 billion, representing growth of approximately 5.7% over the previous year. This revenue supported a net income of roughly $5.0 billion, which reflects the company's ability to remain profitable despite complex global supply chains.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is around 7.9x, indicating that the company uses a significant amount of borrowed money compared to shareholder equity. The current ratio, which measures the ability to cover short-term obligations with current assets, is approximately 1.1x. For the same fiscal year, the company generated free cash flow of about $6.9 billion, providing ample room for shareholder returns among defense stocks.

During FY 2025, revenue reached about $18.7 billion, which was a sharp increase of roughly 33% compared to the prior year. Despite this rapid top-line growth, the company reported a net loss of about $4.9 billion. This underscores the high costs associated with developing next-generation spacecraft and expanding a global satellite constellation.

The company's December 2025 balance sheet shows a debt-to-equity ratio of approximately 0.6x, suggesting a relatively lower reliance on debt relative to its equity. Its current ratio is close to 1.4x, signifying a healthy cushion for meeting short-term financial needs. Note that stock-based compensation (SBC) represented roughly 28.7% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement. Free cash flow for the period was a negative $14.0 billion.

Lockheed Martin faces significant risks from its revenue concentration, as nearly 72% of its 2025 sales came from the U.S. federal government. Any shifts in defense priorities or budget cuts could impact its long-term contracts. Furthermore, the F-35 program accounts for roughly 27% of total revenue, meaning any technical failures for that specific aircraft would be damaging. The company also navigates intense competition from peers like RTX Corp. (RTX -0.60%) for high-stakes government projects.

Space Exploration Technologies operates in a capital-intensive industry where regulatory changes can suddenly halt launch schedules. Competition in the commercial launch sector from established players like Boeing Co. (BA -2.26%) or Northrop Grumman Corp. (NOC -0.66%) could pressure its pricing power. The company also faces immense technical risks, as launch failures can result in significant financial losses and delays in project timelines.

Lockheed Martin appears much more attractively valued based on its Forward P/E, while Space Exploration Technologies carries a significantly higher multiple due to its growth profile.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

SpaceX's various businesses intend to leverage the company's core launch capabilities, starting with reusable rockets. The ability to reuse boosters significantly lowers per-launch costs and spreads fixed manufacturing costs across multiple missions. Expectations are that scaling up quickly will happen, with Wall Street analysts projecting $48.9 billion in sales for fiscal 2026, and a swing to profitability, with $4 billion net income projected.

The lack of free cash flow appears to be crushing; projections indicate free cash flow will be negative $59 billion this year, then jump to negative $146 billion in 2027.

Still, the success of Tesla Inc. (TSLA -7.24%) has made founder Elon Musk the richest man in the world and raised expectations that he can make an even greater fortune from SpaceX. The business certainly has market support behind it, raising $85.7 billion this year through what was at the time the world's largest-ever IPO.

SpaceX has a very real business in Starlink, which mitigates the possibility that grander plans won't come to fruition. But the company doesn't have a monopoly on any of its businesses--there are other space cargo and reusable rocket competitors, other space-based Internet and mobile phone networks, and plenty of AI competitors.

Lockheed Martin Corp. is a core company in U.S. aerospace and defense. In particular, the F-35 fighter program remains a pillar of Lockheed's business, with the Defense Department planning to continue to buy the jet into the 2040s. Having more than a quarter of revenue essentially guaranteed for 15 years or more is unheard of and quite appealing to a long-term investor. In addition to jet fighters, the company has a handful of drone systems it says can integrate into U.S. defense systems to provide a blanket of security systems to complement the jets.

Lockheed's revenue should rise 8% this year to $81 billion, with a much healthier 40% jump in net income to more than $7 billion.

SpaceX has the buzz, but shares come at a sky-high premium. Lockheed Martin's equity is priced at a discount to the S&P 500's average P/E and P/S ratios. That's a good deal for a company that has predictable revenue for the foreseeable future given its role in American defense. Long-term investors should go with Lockheed Martin shares.
